content: Willowbrook State School was a state-funded institution located in Staten Island, New York City, designed to care for children with intellectual disabilities. Construction of Willowbrook State School In 1938, plans were initiated to construct a facility for children with intellectual disabilities on a 375-acre site in the Willowbrook area of Staten Island. The construction was completed in 1942, but instead of being used for its intended purpose, the facility was repurposed as Halloran General Hospital, a U.S. Army hospital named after Colonel Paul Stacey Halloran. After World War II, there were discussions about transferring the site to the Veterans Administration. However, in October 1947, the New York State Department of Mental Hygiene opened the facility as originally planned, naming it Willowbrook State School. Hepatitis Studies at Willowbrook During the first decade of its operation, the school experienced frequent outbreaks of hepatitis. Between 1963 and 1966, a controversial medical study was conducted at the institution. In this study, healthy children were deliberately infected with the hepatitis virus, either orally or via injection, to study the effects of gamma globulin as a treatment. This unethical practice caused public outrage, leading to the termination of the study. Scandals and Abuses at Willowbrook In early 1972, investigative journalist Geraldo Rivera conducted a series of exposés on the conditions at Willowbrook. His investigation revealed appalling circumstances, including severe overcrowding, unsanitary living conditions, and instances of physical and sexual abuse perpetrated by staff members. These revelations followed earlier reports in local newspapers, such as the Staten Island Advance and Staten Island Register. A settlement was reached on May 5, 1975, which mandated significant reforms at the institution. However, it took several years for all the violations to be addressed. The widespread attention generated by this case played a pivotal role in the enactment of the Civil Rights of Institutionalized Persons Act in 1980. In 1983, the state announced plans to close the institution, which had been renamed the Staten Island Developmental Center in 1974. By March 1986, the number of residents had decreased from a peak of 5,000 to just 250. The last residents left the facility on September 17, 1987. In 1989, a portion of the land was acquired by the City of New York to establish a new campus for the College of Staten Island (CSI). The new campus opened in 1993, consolidating CSI’s operations and closing its previous campus in the Sunnyside neighborhood. The new campus, spanning 204 acres, became the largest maintained by the City University of New York (CUNY). The remaining 171 acres of the original Willowbrook property, located at the southern end, remain under the administration of the New York State Department of Mental Hygiene. This area now houses the Institute for Basic Research. On February 25, 1987, the Federal Court approved the 1987 Stipulation, which outlined guidelines for the Office of Mental Retardation and Developmental Disabilities (OMRDD). These guidelines required the placement of members of the Willowbrook class into community-based settings.
